text:
This case is not about an arbitrary deprivation of property, but about the lawful operation of two successive disability-benefit regimes that used different medical concepts and different eligibility rules. The record shows that on 1 December 2009 the applicant was assessed at 40% under the post-2008 methodology, and the full panel report records retained daily-function capacities, possible work adaptation, and a review set for 2012 because her condition was considered stable rather than terminal; that is why her pension was withdrawn from 1 February 2010. When her condition was later assessed at 50% in 2011 and 2012, the authorities still applied the statutory structure consistently: in December 2011 rehabilitation was considered feasible within 36 months, and in 2012 her applications failed because the certified social-security ledger showed only 947 insured days in the preceding five years, not the 1,095 required by Act CXCI of 2011, and she met none of the alternative gateways. Under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the applicant must show more than disappointment at a reform: the interference had a legal basis, pursued a legitimate social-policy aim—confirmed by the reform materials replacing passive benefits with a rehabilitation-centred, contribution-based system—and fell within the State’s margin of appreciation, so no violation should be found.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

This case is about the destruction of an earned social-insurance entitlement by a paper reclassification that did not reflect any real recovery. The applicant had over 23 years of insured employment and was awarded disability pension in 2001 on that contribution record; yet after the 2008 methodological change, her pension of HUF 60,975 per month was withdrawn from 1 February 2010 even though the Labour Court’s own expert, in a report of 16 February 2011, found that the old 67% and new 40% scores were both technically correct under different systems but that her condition had not significantly improved since 2007. The interference with her “possession” under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was therefore disproportionate: the State first removed her pension without any actual rehabilitation, then in 2012 denied her renewed entitlement because she lacked 1,095 insured days in the previous five years—a condition she could hardly satisfy after being pushed out of the labour market by disability and stripped of pension status in 2010. I will show that Hungary upset the fair balance by converting an earned insurance right into a trap: “rehabilitable” on paper, unsupported in reality, and excluded from both the old and new schemes.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

The applicant's social-security coverage ledger for the five years preceding her 20 February 2012 and 15 August 2012 applications, certified by the pension authority, showing day-by-day insured periods, gaps exceeding 30 days, and a total of 947 covered days rather than the required 1,095; this file also contains the formal eligibility checklist used under Act CXCI of 2011, documenting that she failed each alternative gateway under the new statute.

A written response from the county rehabilitation authority to the applicant's 2012 inquiry, confirming that although the December 2011 panel had recommended 'complex rehabilitation within 36 months', no rehabilitation programme, placement, training slot, or rehabilitation allowance was ever opened for her because no implementing measure was initiated by the competent office; this tends to show that she was treated as rehabilitable on paper while receiving none of the substitute support attached to that status.

Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects existing possessions and, in some circumstances, claims sufficiently established in domestic law; it does not guarantee a right to acquire or retain a social-security benefit once the statutory conditions are no longer met. On these facts, the applicant’s pension was lawfully withdrawn after the 1 December 2009 assessment fixed her at 40% under the new methodology, and her later 2012 applications were refused because the certified ledger showed only 947 insured days in the relevant five-year period, not the 1,095 required by Act CXCI of 2011, while she also failed the alternative gateways. Even if there was an interference, it was prescribed by law, pursued a legitimate social-policy aim in reorganising disability support toward rehabilitation and contribution-based eligibility, and remained within the State’s margin of appreciation under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 because the authorities gave concrete reasons tied to medical assessment and contribution history rather than acting arbitrarily.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects not only possessions already being paid, but also sufficiently established social-insurance claims; here the applicant’s pension was an earned insurance entitlement grounded in over 23 years and 71 days of service and contributions, not a mere welfare hope. The decisive proportionality flaw is this: the State terminated her pension from 1 February 2010 on the basis of a methodological reclassification even though the Labour Court’s expert report of 16 February 2011 found no significant medical improvement since 2007, and then, after classifying her in December 2011 as suitable for rehabilitation, provided neither the promised rehabilitation nor the rehabilitation allowance before using Act CXCI of 2011 to reject her 2012 claim for lacking 1,095 insured days. Under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, a State may reform benefits, but it must preserve a fair balance; Hungary did not, because it first removed HUF 60,975 per month without real recovery and then relied on contribution gaps that were the foreseeable consequence of excluding a disabled person from both work and substitute support.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

An internal methodological guidance circular issued by the National Rehabilitation and Social Welfare Authority after the 2008 reform, with conversion examples and explanatory notes showing how prior 'loss of working capacity' percentages were not directly equivalent to the new 'overall health impairment' percentages; the circular includes a worked example indicating that a former 67% incapacity rating would typically map to a materially lower percentage under the new scale, supporting the Government's position that the systems were conceptually different.

A complete copy of the Nyíregyháza Labour Court-appointed medical expert report dated 16 February 2011, including its annexed comparative table, stating that the applicant's 67% loss of working capacity under the pre-2008 rules and 40% health impairment under the post-2008 rules were both methodologically correct but not medically indicative of any substantial improvement; the report further notes persistent spinal, cardiovascular and musculoskeletal limitations and records that no realistic vocational rehabilitation plan had been identified.

The plaintiff’s strongest point is the 16 February 2011 court expert report saying there was no significant medical improvement since 2007, but that does not prove a Convention violation. The issue under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 is not whether her underlying illnesses vanished; it is whether the authorities acted arbitrarily in applying a new, lawful assessment framework and later a new eligibility statute. The methodological circular already on the record shows why 67% under the old 'loss of working capacity' model was not equivalent to 67% under the new 'overall health impairment' model, and the full administrative file shows the authorities then applied the 2012 contribution rules mechanically, not selectively: 947 insured days, not 1,095, with gaps over 30 days and no grandfathering because she was not receiving disability pension or rehabilitation allowance on 31 December 2011. As for the complaint that rehabilitation was never implemented, that may suggest administrative imperfection, but it does not convert a failed statutory prerequisite into a vested property right to disability allowance in 2012, nor does it show that the refusal decisions of 5 June 2012 and 23 November 2012 were unlawful or disproportionate.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 requires a fair balance between the general interest and the individual’s property rights; even where a social-security reform is lawful in abstracto, it becomes disproportionate if it imposes an excessive individual burden. That is exactly what happened here: the applicant’s earned disability pension of HUF 60,975 per month was terminated from 1 February 2010 after a mere methodological reclassification, although the court-appointed expert on 16 February 2011 found no significant medical improvement since 2007, and when the authorities later classified her in December 2011 as fit for 'complex rehabilitation within 36 months', they provided neither the rehabilitation programme nor the rehabilitation allowance attached to that status. The State cannot invoke the 1,095-day rule under Act CXCI of 2011 as if it were neutral when, by its own acts, it had already removed her pension, left her without the substitute rehabilitation support, and thereby made it foreseeable that she would fall short of insured days; under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, that sequence upset the fair balance and placed an excessive burden on this applicant.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

Preparatory materials for Act CXCI of 2011, including an explanatory memorandum and ministry briefing note, stating that the reform aimed to replace passive long-term benefits with a rehabilitation-centred system, tighten contribution-based eligibility, and preserve acquired status only for persons already receiving disability pension or rehabilitation allowance on 31 December 2011; these materials support the contention that the legislative change pursued a general social-policy objective and was not targeted at the applicant individually.

A copy of the 5 June 2012 refusal decision with the underlying insurance-day calculation sheet, together with municipal and employment records showing that the applicant had only a brief public-employment placement in summer 2012 and otherwise lacked opportunities to rebuild insured status after losing her pension in 2010; the file supports the argument that the new 1,095-day condition operated retroactively against someone already outside the labour market because of disability.

Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 is not breached where a social-security entitlement is altered by law in pursuit of a legitimate public-interest reform and the individual no longer satisfies the statutory conditions. Here, the decisive point is that by the time of the impugned 2012 refusals the applicant had no existing entitlement under domestic law: Act CXCI of 2011 required 1,095 insured days in the preceding five years, or uninterrupted cover, or receipt of disability pension/rehabilitation allowance on 31 December 2011, and the certified ledger showed 947 days, gaps exceeding 30 days, and no grandfathered status. Nor was the 2011 'rehabilitable on paper' point enough to create a possession: the 13 December 2011 second-instance decision expressly recorded 50% disability but also that rehabilitation was feasible within 36 months, so disability allowance was not automatically due under the statutory structure; under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the Convention does not convert an unimplemented recommendation for rehabilitation into a vested property right to a different cash benefit.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 protects possessions and requires a fair balance; Article 14 of the Convention, read together with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, forbids materially unjustified differential treatment in the enjoyment of that property right. On these facts, the State created exactly such an arbitrary distinction: persons who happened still to be receiving disability pension or rehabilitation allowance on 31 December 2011 were preserved under Act CXCI of 2011, while this applicant—whose pension had been withdrawn on 1 February 2010 after a methodological reclassification despite the 16 February 2011 court expert finding no significant medical improvement, and who then received neither the promised rehabilitation programme nor rehabilitation allowance after the 13 December 2011 decision—was excluded from all protection. That line was not based on any real difference in medical condition or contribution history: she had 23 years and 71 days of service, was repeatedly assessed at 50% disability in 2011-2012, and yet was denied solely because the State first removed her insured status and substitute support, then invoked the 1,095-day rule against the very gap its own actions had produced.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified); Article 14 of the Convention (verified)]

Minutes and decision sheets from the second-instance authority dated 13 December 2011, stating that the applicant's disability level had risen to 50% but that rehabilitation was regarded as possible within 36 months; the file includes standardised employability factors and notes that disability allowance was not automatically due where rehabilitation remained feasible, indicating that the authorities were applying the statutory structure rather than simply denying support arbitrarily.

The applicant's pension insurance file containing her contribution history and pension award dossier from 2001, including the original disability-pension decision and contribution records showing over two decades of insured employment; attached internal calculation sheets indicate that her entitlement under the old scheme was based on completed service time and medically certified incapacity, supporting her expectation that the pension was an earned social-insurance benefit rather than a discretionary welfare payment.

Under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, the question is not whether the applicant’s illnesses persisted, but whether Hungary acted lawfully and proportionately in changing benefit rules; on this record, it did. The full 1 December 2009 panel report shows why her pension was withdrawn from 1 February 2010: functional testing and physician observations recorded retained daily capacities and potential work adaptation, and the panel set review for 2012 because her condition was considered stable, not terminal—so this was an evidence-based reassessment under a new methodology, not arbitrary confiscation. And when she applied again in 2012, the refusal was dictated by Act CXCI of 2011’s neutral contribution rules: the certified ledger shows only 947 insured days in the preceding five years, with gaps over 30 days, and she was not receiving disability pension or rehabilitation allowance on 31 December 2011, so she failed every statutory gateway.

The plaintiff’s best point is that no rehabilitation was actually implemented after the 13 December 2011 decision, but that cannot manufacture a “possession” the law did not grant: that decision expressly found 50% disability yet rehabilitation feasible within 36 months, meaning disability allowance was not automatically due, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 does not convert an unexecuted rehabilitation recommendation into a vested right to cash benefits. The reform materials confirm a general social-policy aim—moving from passive pensions to rehabilitation and tighter contribution-based eligibility—not a measure targeted at this applicant. The fair-balance test therefore favors the State: lawful medical reassessment in 2009, lawful statutory ineligibility in 2012, and no arbitrariness or disproportionality shown.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]

Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 was violated because Hungary destroyed an earned social-insurance possession without preserving any fair balance: this applicant had over 23 years and 71 days of service, had been paid a disability pension of HUF 60,975 per month since 2001, and yet lost it from 1 February 2010 even though the Labour Court’s own expert on 16 February 2011 found that the old 67% and new 40% ratings were merely products of different methodologies and that her condition had not significantly improved since 2007. That conclusion is confirmed by the treating-physician records from 2007 to 2012, which show continuous spinal, cardiovascular and musculoskeletal problems, ongoing medication, pain, and reduced mobility, with no clinically meaningful recovery at all. The State’s best answer is that the 2012 refusals were simply the neutral application of Act CXCI’s 1,095-day rule, but that ignores causation and proportionality: after stripping her pension in 2010, the authorities classified her on 13 December 2011 as fit for “complex rehabilitation within 36 months,” then provided neither any rehabilitation programme nor the rehabilitation allowance, and finally used the resulting lack of insured days—947 instead of 1,095—to exclude her altogether. A lawful reform in the abstract cannot, under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, be applied so as to leave a repeatedly 50%-disabled insured worker with no pension, no rehabilitation, no substitute allowance, and only token municipal aid; that excessive individual burden is why you should find for the applicant.
[Law-library check: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (verified)]
